Location of the Lhasa terrane in the Late Cretaceous and its implications for
crustal deformation
Yiming Maa,b,c,*, Qiang Wangb,d,e,*, Tianshui Yangf, Quan Oug, Xiuzheng Zhangb, Wei Danb,
Shihong Zhangf, Huaichun Wuf, Haiyan Lif, Liwan Caof, Jun Wangb, Di Zoua,c, Huapei Wangc
aSchool of Earth Sciences, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan 430074, China
bState Key Laboratory of Isotope Geochemistry, Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Guangzhou 510640, China
cPaleomagnetism and Planetary Magnetism Laboratory, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan 430074, China
dCAS Center for Excellence in Tibetan Plateau Earth Sciences, Beijing 100101, China
eCollege of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 10049, China
fState Key Laboratory of Biogeology and Environmental Geology, China University of Geosciences, Beijing 100083, China

A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T
Editor: Howard Falcon-Lang The Cenozoic crustal deformation of the Asian continent is constrained by the location of its southern margin in
the Late Cretaceous, which is, however, affected by potential remagnetization and inclination shallowing of
Keywords: redbeds in the Linzhou Basin. Our paleomagnetic results from the Shexing Formation redbeds in the Late
Tibetan Plateau Cretaceous yield a mean paleo-inclination of ~21.5◦, consistent with the recalculation of previous data. Rock-
Paleomagnetism
magnetic, paleomagnetic and petrographic analyses indicate that the redbeds have recorded the original
Northward movement
paleomagnetic field and have not suffered from significant inclination shallowing. The paleopole from 70 red-

beds sites is at 71.8◦N, 281.5◦E with A95 =2.6◦, yielding a paleolatitude of ~12.0 ±2.6◦N at ~70–91 Ma for the
Linzhou Basin. This result indicates a latitudinal convergence of 1264 ±477 km north of the sampling area
within Asia since the Late Cretaceous. Combined with previous data, our results show that the southern margin of
Asia was at ~11–15◦N in the Late Cretaceous, aligning in a WNW-ESE direction, which is similar to its present-
day orientation. A review of available data shows that the sharp bending of the southern margin of Asia around
the eastern Himalayan syntaxis (EHS) is probably due to different crustal movement patterns around the EHS.
The shape of the southern margin of Asia determines the arc-shaped orientation of Himalayan orogen.

Fig. 1. (a, b) Regional geological map of the Tibetan Plateau and adjacent areas, modified from Yin and Harrison (2000) and Li et al. (2015). Abbreviations: BST,
Baoshan terrane; NCB, North China block; QTNK, Qimen Tagh-North Kunlun thrust system; SCB, South China block; STB, Shan-Thai block; TCT, Tengchong terrane;
EHS, eastern Himalayan syntaxis; WHS, western Himalayan syntaxis. (c) Geological map of the sampling area, modified from Tan et al. (2010) based on our
observation. 1, stratigraphic units including P2p (Upper Permian Pangna Fm), K1l (Lower Cretaceous Linbuzong Fm), K1ch (Lower Cretaceous Chumulong Fm), K1-2t
(Cretaceous Takena Fm), K2sh (Upper Cretaceous Shexing Fm), E1d (Paleocene Dianzhong Fm), E2n (Eocene Nianbo Fm), E2p (Eocene Pana Fm) and Q (Quaternary).
2, intrusive units. 3, strike and dip of bedding. 4, town. 5, Sampling locations of Tan et al. (2010) (black dots) and this study (red dots). (For interpretation of the
references to color in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.)

The similarities of the magmatism, stratigraphy, paleobiogeography convergence, including crustal shortening and thickening accommo-
of the Tengchong and Lhasa terranes suggest that there has been a dated by the Cenozoic fold and thrust belts within Asia since the colli-
sion (e.g., van Hinsbergen et al., 2011) and the lateral extrusion of
crustal materials around the southeastern edge of the Tibetan Plateau
since the Oligocene (e.g., Tong et al., 2017a). The difference between
the observed paleolatitude and the expected one calculated from the
reference pole is the latitudinal convergence within Asia north of the
study area. The observed paleolatitudes for the reference point RPW
(31.7◦N, 80.1◦E) and RPC (29.3◦N, 91.1◦E) are ~15.2◦N and ~ 11.4◦N,
respectively, while the expected paleolatitudes calculated from the
reference pole of East Asia at 80 Ma are 23.8◦ ± 3.4◦N and 22.8◦ ±
3.4◦N, respectively (Cogn´e et al., 2013). The paleolatitude differences
between the paleolatitude observed at 80 Ma and that expected at 80 Ma
are ~8.6◦ and ~ 11.4◦ for the reference point (31.7◦N, 80.1◦E) and
(29.3◦N, 91.1◦E), respectively. These results reveal that the latitudinal
convergences are ~1000 km and ~ 1300 km, respectively, for the
western and central parts within Asia since 80 Ma. Therefore, there was
no significant crustal convergence difference within Asia north of the
Indus-Tsangpo suture zone between the western and central part of the
Tibetan Plateau at the paleomagnetic confidence level (Ma et al., 2017a,
2017b).
The amount of crustal convergence is consistent with that of crustal
shortening of ~1000 km absorbed by the Cenozoic thrust and fold belts
within Asia (Ma et al., 2014, 2017b; Yin and Harrison, 2000; van
Hinsbergen et al., 2011), indicating that most of the crustal convergence
is crustal shortening. The difference between the most probable amounts
of the latitudinal convergence of the central and western parts may be
explained by the lateral extrusions of crustal material, which plays a
more critical role in the central and eastern parts of the Tibetan Plateau
than those in the western part (Otofuji et al., 2007; Tong et al., 2016,
2017a).

areas are oceans. The yellow terranes in panels (b) were reconstructed using the observed paleolatitudes, while the pink terranes show the expected paleolatitudes.
